payload.title: What Are the Palestinian Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
payload.audience: Couples in their 30s interested in destination weddings and luxury experiences, AUD 150k+ budget
payload.reader: An Australian couple in their 30s where one or both partners have Palestinian roots (Muslim or Christian family), or a mixed-heritage couple, who want to honour those customs at a destination wedding outside Palestine or at home in Australia, and need to know what each custom involves, what it means, and what it asks of a venue (space for a zaffeh and dabke, live music, a shared feast).
payload.goal: Read the free Wedded Wonderland digital magazine (primary CTA); secondary, in-context invitation to speak with a Wedded Advisor placed straight after the 'Bringing these customs to your destination wedding' section.
payload.service_link: /magazine (primary, UTM-tagged); /wonderland-concierge (secondary, UTM-tagged, after the destination planning section)
payload.angle: Page-one listicles flatten Palestinian weddings into one generic 'Arab wedding' and repeat the same five customs without sources. We follow the order of a real Palestinian wedding (the asking, the engagement, the henna night, the day, the feast), source each meaning to UNESCO, museum dress collections, the Palestinian Museum and academic or encyclopaedia references, say plainly which customs belong to Muslim families, which to Christian families and which are shared, and add what the listicles skip: Smartraveller currently says do not travel to Palestine (updated 14 September 2026), so we show couples how to carry these customs into a wedding elsewhere or in Australia, with the venue planning points that make a zaffeh, dabke and sahja work.
must_include: Exactly 4 one-sentence Key takeaways at the top.
The 12 customs in tradition_plan (batch A and batch B), each with a sourced meaning; unsourced origins labelled 'often told' or left out.

Faith clarity: katb al-kitab and mahr framed as Muslim family customs; church customs framed as Christian family customs; henna, tatreez, zaffeh, zaghareet, dabke, sahja and the feast shown as shared where sources say so. No custom presented as universal or religious unless sourced.

Tatreez section anchored on the UNESCO Representative List inscription (2021, 'The art of embroidery in Palestine, practices, skills, knowledge and rituals'), with regional dress variation only where a museum or the Palestinian Museum states it.

A 'Bringing these customs to your destination wedding' section: Smartraveller's current Do not travel advice for Palestine stated once, factually, with its date; then venue planning points (dance floor size and surface for dabke, live tabl and mizmar or a band and sound limits, a processional route for the zaffeh, catering for a shared feast, a separate henna night space). No named venues or vendors.
Timeline grouping: before the day (batch A) and the wedding day and celebration (batch B).

Internal links: pillar /expert-advice/wedding-traditions in intro and close; /guides/arab-wedding-traditions, /guides/muslim-wedding-traditions, /7-big-and-electrifying-lebanese-wedding-traditions in context.
Short FAQ (5 to 6 questions) from SEO People Also Ask, answered only with sourced facts.
Primary CTA to /magazine and secondary Wedded Advisor CTA after the destination section; Advisor claims only from brand-facts.md.

tradition_plan.note: Planner fact-checks in 2 parallel batches, 15 min hard. Preferred sources: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (ich.unesco.org), the Palestinian Museum (palmuseum.org, including its dress and embroidery exhibitions), museums with Palestinian dress collections (e.g. British Museum, Victoria and Albert Museum, Penn Museum, Museum of International Folk Art, Ashmolean, Palestine Heritage Center), Britannica and Oxford reference works, peer-reviewed ethnomusicology and anthropology sources. Place names and terms follow the sources. Culture, not politics. If a fact cannot be found in time: mark 'often told' or drop it. No extra sourcing rounds.

facts_to_source: Jaha is the delegation of respected men from the groom's family who visit the bride's family (old page wrongly calls it a single elder or mediator)
Tulbeh as the formal request for the bride's hand
Coffee custom at the asking (often told that the coffee is drunk once the answer is given): source or label 'often told'
Sweets and agreement of terms: only if sourced

batch_A.tradition: Katb al-kitab (the marriage contract) and the engagement
facts_to_source: What katb al-kitab is (signing the Islamic marriage contract, often before the wedding celebration)
Who is present (imam or official, witnesses)
Christian engagement equivalent (betrothal, ring blessing) only if a source describes it for Palestinian Christian families
Mahr as the bride's right in an Islamic marriage contract, paid or promised by the groom
Drop the old page's 'gift or dowry' and 'groom's family carries much of the cost' unless sourced
No amounts or customary figures
Night or days before the wedding; henna applied to the bride and sometimes guests
Whether it is women only (old page says 'strictly'): source or soften
Songs sung at the henna night, if sourced
Groom's own henna, regional, only if sourced
UNESCO 2021 inscription: name, year, what it says about embroidery and social meaning
Motifs and colours varying by region or village (Palestinian Museum or museum collection page)
Wedding dresses specifically (e.g. a bride's thobe or trousseau): source or omit
Drop 'black or white with red patterns' as a universal description
Licensed textile photo only (visual curator)
Groom washed and shaved by friends on the wedding day, with songs
Whether it is village or regional: only if sourced
If no source in time: label 'often told' or drop and promote an optional item
Procession bringing the groom or couple with music
Instruments named in sources (tabl, mizmar or others)
Groom lifted on shoulders: source or drop
Venue note: needs a route and space (no source needed for planning advice)
What it is, who performs it, when in the celebrations
Short rhymed lines sung before the ululation (ahazeej), if sourced
Line or circle dance, stamping steps, held hands or shoulders
Lead dancer (lawweeh) role, if sourced
Check whether any UNESCO listing covers dabke for Palestine; do not claim one unless confirmed
Drop 'it's not an Arab party without a dabke'
Sahja (or sahjeh): men's celebration with clapping, singing and poetry, often the night before
Sung poetry forms named in sources (e.g. zajal, ataaba, dal'ouna) and their role
Groom's and bride's song traditions only where sourced
Shared feast as hospitality; dishes named only if a source ties them to Palestinian weddings
Who hosts which meal: only if sourced
Drop 'several days' unless sourced
Church wedding customs of Palestinian Christian families, e.g. the crowning in Orthodox rites, as described by a church, museum, encyclopaedia or academic source
Which churches (Orthodox, Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran) only as sources state
If nothing Palestinian-specific is found in time: one sourced sentence that Christian families marry in church and share the celebration customs, with no detail invented

optional_if_sourced: Nuqut (gifts of money to the couple, no amounts)
The bride's procession to the groom's home (tal'at al-'aroos)
Bride's trousseau (jihaz) and gold jewellery, no prices
dropped_from_old_page: Refugee and diaspora framing in the intro: political, drop
'Every Arab' and 'not an Arab party without' generalisations
Unrelated 'Venues & Vendors to Explore' block (template, not body)

avoid: Political commentary, conflict narrative or territorial claims; Smartraveller is cited only as travel advice, once.
Suggesting a wedding in Palestine, or naming an alternative destination without first checking its current Smartraveller level.
Presenting every custom as Islamic or as universal; mixing Palestinian customs with generic 'Arab' ones.
Reusing wording, structure or image captions from the old page; reusing its images (licence unknown).
AI images of people, cultural dress or ceremonies; tatreez only as a licensed textile photo.
Prices, mahr or gift amounts, and vendor or venue names.
Competitor branding or copy; em dashes; US spelling.
